categoryBlurb: Seafood is the fastest good dinner there is — most of these are done in the time it takes to boil water, and the rest are the kind of weekend pot that makes the whole apartment smell like a harbor town.

recipes.title: Pan-Seared Scallops with Brown Butter
recipes.blurb: A deep golden crust on top, a barely-set sweet center, and a nutty brown butter pan sauce you spoon over at the last second. It is a restaurant plate that takes ten minutes.

items: 1 lb (450 g) dry-packed sea scallops (U-10 or U-12 size, about 10-12 scallops)
1 tbsp (15 ml) grapeseed or avocado oil
4 tbsp (55 g) unsalted butter, cut into 4 pieces
1 tbsp (15 ml) fresh lemon juice, plus 1/2 tsp finely grated zest
2 tbsp (8 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1/4 tsp flaky sea salt, for finishing

instructions.title: Buy the right scallops
instructions.text: Ask for dry-packed or dry sea scallops, which are sold without the phosphate solution that wet scallops swim in. Wet scallops look bright white and sit in milky liquid, and they will steam instead of sear no matter how hot your pan is. Dry scallops look slightly ivory or pinkish and feel tacky. This one purchase decision matters more than anything else you do tonight.

instructions.title: Remove the side muscle
instructions.text: Look along the side of each scallop for a small rectangular tab of firmer, slightly fibrous flesh. Pinch it and peel it away with your fingers — it comes off easily and takes two seconds per scallop. That muscle turns rubbery and chewy when cooked, so pulling it off is the difference between tender and stringy.

instructions.title: Dry them hard
instructions.text: Lay the scallops on a plate lined with a double layer of paper towels, then press another towel firmly on top. Let them sit uncovered for 10 minutes, changing the towel once if it soaks through. Surface water has to boil off before browning can start, and every drop you remove now is a second of searing you get back later. They should feel dry and slightly sticky to the touch.

instructions.title: Season at the last minute
instructions.text: Season the scallops with the 1 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper right before they hit the pan, not a moment earlier. Salt pulls moisture to the surface within a minute or two, which undoes all the drying you just did. Set the seasoned scallops near the stove so you can move fast.

instructions.title: Get the pan properly hot
instructions.text: Set a 12 in (30 cm) stainless steel or cast iron skillet over medium-high heat for 2-3 minutes, then add the 1 tbsp oil and swirl. The oil should shimmer and thin out, moving like water, with the first faint wisp of smoke. If it is billowing smoke, pull the pan off the heat for 30 seconds — too hot scorches the sugars before the inside warms through. Avoid nonstick here; it does not hold enough heat to build a real crust.

instructions.title: Sear side one and do not touch
instructions.text: Lay the scallops in the pan one at a time, working clockwise so you know which went in first, and leave at least 1 in (2.5 cm) between them. Crowding drops the pan temperature and traps steam. Do not move, poke, or peek for a full 2 to 3 minutes — you should hear a steady aggressive sizzle, not a quiet hiss. When the bottom edge has gone deep amber, they will release from the pan on their own.

instructions.title: Flip and finish fast
instructions.text: Flip each scallop with tongs or a thin fish spatula and cook just 60 to 90 seconds on the second side. A 1 1/2 in (4 cm) scallop needs about 4 minutes of total cooking, and the second side is only there to set it. Press the side gently: it should feel like the fleshy pad below your thumb, with a little give. Overcooked scallops feel firm and springy like a rubber eraser.

instructions.title: Rest them off the heat
instructions.text: Move the scallops to a warm plate, seared side up, and let them sit while you make the sauce. They carry over about 5°F (3°C) as they rest, drifting from 125°F to 130°F (52°C to 54°C) in the center, which is exactly where they are sweet and just barely translucent. Do not tent them with foil — trapped steam will soften the crust you just worked for.

instructions.title: Brown the butter
instructions.text: Turn the heat to medium, add the 4 tbsp butter to the same pan, and swirl constantly as it melts and foams. In 2 to 3 minutes the foam will subside, the milk solids on the bottom will turn the color of a hazelnut, and it will smell toasty and sweet. Brown butter goes from perfect to burnt in about 20 seconds, so keep the pan moving and trust your nose more than your eyes.

instructions.title: Finish the sauce off heat
instructions.text: Pull the pan off the burner, add the sliced garlic and swirl for 30 seconds in the residual heat so it perfumes the butter without scorching. Stir in the 1 tbsp lemon juice, the zest, the capers if using, and the parsley — the lemon will hiss and cut the richness. Taste and add a pinch more salt if it needs it.

instructions.title: Plate and serve immediately
instructions.text: Arrange the scallops seared side up on warm plates and spoon the brown butter over and around them, making sure the browned bits get divided fairly. Finish with the 1/4 tsp flaky salt. Scallops wait for no one — serve them within a minute or two, while the crust is still crisp against the soft center.

tips: If your scallops release a puddle of liquid the second they hit the pan, they were wet-packed. Pour off the liquid, let the pan get hot again, and finish them — you will get flavor but not much crust.
Sear in two batches rather than crowding a small pan. Two perfect batches beat one steamed one, and the second batch cooks in the flavorful fat from the first.
No thermometer works well on something this thin — go by feel and by the clock. Four minutes total for 1 1/2 in scallops, five for anything bigger.
Brown butter can be made up to a week ahead and refrigerated. Rewarm it gently and add the lemon and herbs fresh, since acid and parsley fade fast.
Serve over creamy polenta, pea puree, or just good bread — you want something to catch the butter.
recipes.keyTemp: Pull at 125-130°F (52-54°C) in the center for sweet, just-set scallops; the FDA guideline for fully cooked shellfish is 145°F (63°C), which will be firmer.
recipes.pairing: A cold glass of unoaked Chardonnay or Sancerre, with crusty bread and a simple arugula salad.

recipes.title: Garlic Butter Shrimp Scampi
recipes.blurb: Shrimp, a lot of garlic, white wine, lemon, and enough butter to make a sauce worth mopping up. This is the twenty-minute dinner you will make more than any other recipe in this chapter.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) large shrimp (16-20 count), peeled and deveined, tails on
6 tbsp (85 g) unsalted butter, cut into pieces
1/2 cup (120 ml) dry white wine such as Pinot Grigio or Sauvignon Blanc
3 tbsp (45 ml) fresh lemon juice, plus 1 tsp grated zest
1/4 cup (10 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 baguette (about 12 oz / 340 g), sliced and toasted, for serving

instructions.title: Thaw and dry the shrimp
instructions.text: If your shrimp are frozen, put them in a colander under cold running water for 5 minutes, or in a bowl of cold water for 15 — never in warm water, which starts cooking the outside. Spread them on a towel-lined sheet pan and blot the tops dry as well. Wet shrimp drop the pan temperature and boil in their own liquid instead of picking up any color.

instructions.title: Season and let them sit
instructions.text: Toss the dried shrimp with the 1 tsp kosher salt, 1/2 tsp black pepper, and 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes in a bowl. Let them sit for 10 minutes at room temperature while you slice the garlic and squeeze the lemon. Slightly less-than-fridge-cold shrimp cook more evenly in the 90 seconds per side they get.

instructions.title: Slice the garlic, do not mince it
instructions.text: Thinly slice all 8 cloves rather than mincing them. Minced garlic has more cut surface and burns in a hot pan in under a minute, turning bitter and gritty. Slices hold their shape, sweeten as they cook, and end up as little tender chips in the sauce.

instructions.title: Heat the skillet
instructions.text: Set a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high heat and add the 2 tbsp olive oil. When the oil shimmers and a single shrimp laid in the pan sizzles immediately and steadily, you are ready. If it screams and smokes, back the heat down a notch — you want a confident sizzle, not a scorch.

instructions.title: Sear the shrimp in one layer
instructions.text: Lay the shrimp in the pan in a single layer without crowding, working in two batches if your pan is smaller than 12 in. Cook 60 to 90 seconds per side, until the bottoms are pink with a few golden spots and the flesh has just turned opaque at the edge. They will still be slightly underdone in the center and that is intentional — they finish in the sauce.

instructions.title: Get them out of the pan
instructions.text: Transfer the shrimp to a clean plate the moment the second side turns pink, and do not stack them in a pile. Shrimp go from tender to rubbery in about 30 seconds of extra heat, and the residual heat in a crowded plate keeps cooking them. This pull-and-return method is the single biggest reason home scampi comes out tough.

instructions.title: Sweat the garlic in butter
instructions.text: Lower the heat to medium, add 2 tbsp of the butter to the empty skillet, and add the sliced garlic. Stir constantly for 45 to 60 seconds, until the garlic is fragrant and just barely blonde at the edges. The second you see it turning tan, move to the next step — brown garlic tastes bitter and you cannot fix it.

instructions.title: Deglaze with wine
instructions.text: Pour in the 1/2 cup white wine and scrape the bottom of the pan with a wooden spoon to lift the browned bits, which are pure shrimp flavor. Simmer briskly for 2 to 3 minutes until the liquid has reduced by about half and no longer smells sharply of alcohol. If you skip this reduction the sauce tastes boozy and thin.

instructions.title: Build the butter sauce
instructions.text: Turn the heat to low and whisk in the remaining 4 tbsp butter one piece at a time, adding the next only when the last has melted. Adding cold butter slowly to a gently simmering liquid emulsifies it into a glossy sauce instead of a greasy slick. Stir in the 3 tbsp lemon juice and the zest, then taste for salt.

instructions.title: Return the shrimp and warm through
instructions.text: Slide the shrimp and any juices on the plate back into the pan and toss for 30 to 60 seconds, just long enough to heat them and coat them. They are done when they have curled into a loose C shape and are opaque all the way through. A tight O shape means they went too far.

instructions.title: Finish and serve
instructions.text: Kill the heat, scatter the 1/4 cup parsley over the top, and give one last toss. Serve straight from the skillet with plenty of toasted baguette for the sauce, or spoon it over 1 lb of cooked linguine if you want to stretch it to six people. Eat it right away — the sauce is at its best in the first ten minutes.

tips: Buy shrimp with the shells on and peel them yourself if you have five extra minutes. Simmer the shells in the white wine for 10 minutes, strain, and use that wine for the sauce — it doubles the depth.
No wine in the house? Use 1/2 cup (120 ml) chicken or seafood stock plus 1 extra tsp of lemon juice. Do not use cooking wine, which is heavily salted.
If the sauce breaks and looks oily, pull it off the heat and whisk in 1 tbsp (15 ml) of cold water or a small cube of cold butter to bring it back together.
The shrimp can be peeled, seasoned, and refrigerated up to 6 hours ahead. Everything else comes together in the time it takes to toast the bread.
Frozen shrimp are almost always a better buy than thawed shrimp at the counter, which were frozen and thawed for you at some unknown hour.
recipes.keyTemp: Shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C) — opaque throughout and curled into a loose C. A tight O means overcooked.
recipes.pairing: The same dry white you cooked with, plus a green salad and a lot of bread.

recipes.title: Maryland Crab Cakes with Remoulade
recipes.blurb: Almost all crab, barely any filler, held together with just enough binder to survive the pan. Make them once and you will never order crab cakes out again.

items: 1 lb (450 g) jumbo lump crabmeat, picked over for shell
2 tbsp (8 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
3/4 cup (40 g) panko breadcrumbs, or 12 saltine crackers finely crushed
2 tbsp (30 g) unsalted butter plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) neutral oil, for frying
1 tbsp (15 g) whole grain or Creole mustard
1 tbsp (10 g) minced cornichons or dill pickle
2 tsp (10 ml) hot sauce such as Crystal or Tabasco

instructions.title: Make the remoulade first
instructions.text: Stir the 3/4 cup mayonnaise, mustard, 1 tbsp lemon juice, cornichons, shallot, hot sauce, capers, smoked paprika, and 1/4 tsp salt together in a small bowl. Cover and refrigerate while you make the cakes — 30 minutes minimum, and it is better the next day. The raw shallot mellows and the flavors marry into something that tastes like a sauce rather than a list of ingredients.

instructions.title: Pick through the crab gently
instructions.text: Spread the 1 lb crabmeat on a sheet pan and run your fingertips through it, feeling for shards of shell and cartilage, which are common even in expensive containers. Lift and separate rather than stirring, keeping the big lumps whole. Those intact lumps are the entire point of a good crab cake, and every time you stir you break them down into shreds.

instructions.title: Whisk the binder separately
instructions.text: In a large bowl, whisk the beaten egg, 1/4 cup mayonnaise, Dijon, Worcestershire, Old Bay, 1 tsp lemon juice, and parsley until completely smooth. Mixing the wet ingredients before the crab goes in means you only have to fold two or three times at the end. This is the trick that keeps the lumps intact.

instructions.title: Fold in the crab and panko
instructions.text: Add the crab and the 3/4 cup panko to the bowl and fold with a rubber spatula, scooping from the bottom and turning over, no more than 5 or 6 strokes. Stop the second everything looks moistened, even if it seems loose. The mixture should just barely hold when squeezed; a mixture that packs like meatloaf has too much binder and will taste like bread.

instructions.title: Shape and chill
instructions.text: Divide the mixture into 8 portions of about 3 oz (85 g) each and shape into pucks roughly 3 in (7.5 cm) wide and 1 in (2.5 cm) thick, handling them as little as possible. Set them on a parchment-lined sheet pan, cover, and refrigerate at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours. Chilling firms the mayonnaise and egg so the cakes hold together in the pan — skip it and they will fall apart.

instructions.title: Heat the pan and fat
instructions.text: Set a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron or heavy stainless skillet over medium heat and add the 2 tbsp butter and 1 tbsp oil. The oil keeps the butter from burning while the butter does the browning. When the foam subsides and a stray breadcrumb sizzles steadily, the pan is ready — medium heat, not high, because these need time for the center to warm through.

instructions.title: Fry the first side
instructions.text: Lay 4 cakes in the pan with at least 1 in (2.5 cm) between them and cook undisturbed for 4 to 5 minutes. You are looking for a deep golden brown crust that comes up the sides about a quarter inch. Do not press them down with the spatula — squashing them pushes out the moisture that keeps the inside sweet and tender.

instructions.title: Flip carefully
instructions.text: Slide a thin spatula all the way under each cake, supporting it with your fingers or a second spatula, and turn it in one confident motion. Hesitating is what breaks crab cakes. Cook the second side 3 to 4 minutes, until equally browned and heated through to 145°F (63°C) in the center.

instructions.title: Drain and repeat
instructions.text: Move the finished cakes to a wire rack set over a sheet pan rather than onto paper towels, which trap steam and soften the crust. Wipe out any burnt crumbs, add another tablespoon of butter, and cook the second batch the same way. Keep the first batch warm in a 200°F (95°C) oven for up to 20 minutes.

instructions.title: Serve with lemon and remoulade
instructions.text: Plate two cakes per person with a generous spoonful of the chilled remoulade and a lemon wedge. Squeeze the lemon right before eating — the acid wakes up the sweetness of the crab. A pile of dressed greens on the side is all these need.

tips: Jumbo lump is best but expensive. Backfin or lump is a fine, cheaper choice; skip claw meat, which is dark and stringy for cakes, and never use imitation crab here.
Shaped, uncooked cakes freeze beautifully. Freeze solid on a sheet pan, bag them, and cook from frozen over medium-low heat, adding 3-4 minutes per side.
To broil instead of fry, brush the tops with melted butter and broil 6 in (15 cm) from the element for 8-10 minutes, no flipping.
If your first cake breaks apart in the pan, fold 2 more tbsp of panko into the remaining mixture and chill another 15 minutes before trying again.
The remoulade doubles as a sandwich spread and a dip for fried shrimp — make a full batch even if you only need half.
recipes.keyTemp: Crabmeat is already cooked; heat the cakes to 145°F (63°C) in the center, with a deep golden crust on both sides.
recipes.pairing: A crisp lager or dry Riesling, with corn on the cob or a simple tomato salad.

recipes.title: Broiled Lobster Tails with Drawn Butter
recipes.blurb: Butterflied so the meat sits proud of the shell, brushed with butter, and under the broiler for eight minutes. It looks like a celebration and cooks faster than a baked potato.

items: 4 lobster tails, 6-8 oz (170-225 g) each, thawed if frozen
8 tbsp (115 g) unsalted butter, cut into pieces
1 lemon (about 4 oz / 115 g), cut into wedges

instructions.title: Thaw the tails properly
instructions.text: Move frozen tails to the refrigerator the night before, or seal them in a bag and submerge in cold water for 30 to 45 minutes, changing the water once. Never thaw lobster in warm water or the microwave, which turns the delicate outer layer to mush before the center is even soft. Fully thawed tails feel pliable and the meat springs back when pressed.

instructions.title: Cut the top shell
instructions.text: Set a tail belly-down on a cutting board and use sturdy kitchen shears to cut down the center of the top shell, from the wide open end to the base of the tail fan, stopping just before the fan itself. Cut through the shell only, not deep into the meat. Kitchen shears are worth digging out — a knife slips on the curved shell and this is how people cut themselves.

instructions.title: Butterfly the meat
instructions.text: Spread the shell open with your thumbs until you hear it crack, then slide your fingers underneath the meat and lift it up and out so it rests on top of the closed shell, leaving it attached at the tail fan. Press the empty shell halves back together underneath it. This piggyback presentation is what restaurants do, and it also lifts the meat closer to the broiler so it cooks evenly.

instructions.title: Score and season
instructions.text: Run a knife 1/4 in (6 mm) deep down the length of the exposed meat to help it cook evenly and open slightly as it heats. Rinse away the dark vein if you see one and pat the meat dry with a paper towel. Season all over with the 1 tsp kosher salt and 1/4 tsp pepper.

instructions.title: Mix the garlic butter
instructions.text: Stir the 4 tbsp melted butter with the grated garlic, 1/2 tsp paprika, and 1 tbsp lemon juice in a small bowl. Grating the garlic instead of mincing it means no chunks that can scorch under the broiler. Brush about two thirds of this mixture generously over the exposed meat, letting it pool in the split shell.

instructions.title: Set up the broiler
instructions.text: Position an oven rack so the top of the lobster meat will sit 5 to 6 in (13-15 cm) below the broiler element and preheat the broiler on high for a full 5 minutes. A cold broiler will not brown the butter or spot the meat. Arrange the tails on a foil-lined rimmed sheet pan, spaced 2 in (5 cm) apart.

instructions.title: Broil and watch
instructions.text: Broil for 8 to 10 minutes for 6-8 oz tails, roughly 1 minute per ounce, without flipping. Stay in the kitchen and look through the oven door at the 6 minute mark — broilers vary wildly and butter can go from golden to black quickly. The shells will turn bright red-orange and the meat will puff slightly and turn opaque white.

instructions.title: Check for doneness
instructions.text: Slide an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of the tail from the side; it should read 140°F (60°C) for the classic tender texture, and the FDA guideline for fully cooked shellfish is 145°F (63°C). The meat should be opaque and pearly white all the way through with no translucent gray in the center. Pull them the moment they hit temperature, because lobster carries over and turns tough and squeaky fast.

instructions.title: Make the drawn butter
instructions.text: While the tails broil, melt the 8 tbsp butter in a small saucepan over low heat without stirring and let it sit for 2 minutes. The white milk solids sink and the foam rises; skim the foam and pour off the clear golden butter, leaving the milky layer behind. Season with the 1/2 tsp salt — this is drawn butter, and it stays clear and rich instead of going cloudy.

instructions.title: Finish and serve hot
instructions.text: Brush the tails with the reserved garlic butter, scatter the 1 tbsp parsley over the top, and serve immediately with the drawn butter in small warm bowls and lemon wedges alongside. Lobster loses its magic as it cools, so get it to the table straight from the oven. Give everyone a small fork and permission to use their fingers.

tips: Cold-water tails from Maine or Canada are firmer and sweeter than warm-water tails, which can be mushy. If the packaging does not say, look for tails with clean white meat and no yellowing.
If the tails are larger than 8 oz (225 g), broil 6 in (15 cm) away for 10-12 minutes and check the temperature early — thickness matters more than weight.
Squeaky, rubbery lobster is overcooked lobster. There is no fixing it, so buy a thermometer and pull at 140°F (60°C).
Save the shells in the freezer. Simmered with onion, celery, and water for 45 minutes, they make a stock that turns a basic bisque or the cioppino in this chapter into something special.
Warm the serving plates in a 200°F (95°C) oven for a few minutes so the butter does not congeal on the plate.
recipes.keyTemp: Broil to 140°F (60°C) at the thickest part for tender lobster; 145°F (63°C) is the FDA fully-cooked guideline. Meat should be opaque white with no translucent center.
recipes.pairing: Buttery Chardonnay or Champagne, with roasted asparagus and a baked potato.

recipes.title: Crispy-Skin Pan-Seared Salmon
recipes.blurb: Skin like a potato chip, flesh still rosy and silky in the middle. Once you learn the press-and-wait trick, this is a fifteen-minute dinner you can make half asleep.

items: 4 skin-on salmon fillets, 6 oz (170 g) each, about 1 in (2.5 cm) thick
1 tbsp (15 ml) grapeseed, avocado, or other neutral high-heat oil
1 lemon (about 4 oz / 115 g), half juiced and half cut into wedges
1/2 tsp flaky sea salt, for finishing

instructions.title: Take the chill off
instructions.text: Unwrap the fillets and let them sit at room temperature for 15 minutes before cooking. Ice-cold fish hitting a hot pan seizes up, cooks unevenly, and takes long enough that the outside overcooks before the middle warms. Fifteen minutes on the counter is safe and makes a noticeable difference in how evenly the fillet cooks.

instructions.title: Dry the skin obsessively
instructions.text: Blot both sides with paper towels, then go back to the skin side and press hard with a fresh towel until it feels almost papery. If you have the time, leave the fillets uncovered on a rack in the fridge for 30 minutes. Crisp skin is a moisture problem before it is a heat problem, and damp skin sticks to the pan and tears.

instructions.title: Check for pin bones
instructions.text: Run your fingertips along the center line of each fillet from the thick end toward the tail. If you feel the tips of small bones, pull them straight out with fish tweezers or clean needle-nose pliers, angling in the direction they point. It takes a minute now and saves an unpleasant surprise at the table.

instructions.title: Season right before cooking
instructions.text: Season both sides with the 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper immediately before the fish goes in the pan. Salting early draws beads of moisture to the surface of the skin, which is exactly what you have spent the last ten minutes fighting. Salt the skin a touch more heavily than the flesh — it seasons the crust.

instructions.title: Heat the pan correctly
instructions.text: Set a 12 in (30 cm) stainless steel or cast iron skillet over medium-high heat for 2 minutes, add the 1 tbsp oil, and swirl to coat. When the oil shimmers and moves like water with the first wisp of smoke, it is ready. Nonstick works in a pinch but will never give you the same crackling skin, since it cannot take this level of heat.

instructions.title: Lay the fish in away from you
instructions.text: Place each fillet skin side down, laying it into the pan away from your body so any splatter goes the other direction. Immediately press the top of each fillet firmly with a flexible spatula for 20 to 30 seconds. Salmon skin contracts the second it meets heat and curls the fillet into an arch, and this brief press keeps the whole skin flat against the pan.

instructions.title: Leave it alone
instructions.text: Cook skin side down for 4 to 5 minutes without moving the fish — this is about 70 percent of the total cooking time. Listen for a steady, even sizzle; if it goes quiet, raise the heat slightly, and if it starts spitting violently and smoking, lower it. Watch the side of the fillet: you will see the opaque pink line creep up from the bottom, and you want it about two thirds of the way up before you flip.

instructions.title: Flip and add the butter
instructions.text: Turn the fillets with a thin spatula — properly crisped skin releases without a fight — and add the 2 tbsp butter, thyme sprigs, and smashed garlic to the pan. The butter will foam immediately and start smelling nutty within a minute. Cook the second side just 1 to 2 minutes.

instructions.title: Baste the top
instructions.text: Tilt the pan toward you so the butter pools at the near edge and spoon it over the fillets continuously for about 60 seconds. Basting cooks the top gently with hot fat instead of direct pan heat, so the fish stays moist while it picks up the thyme and garlic. If the butter starts to smell burnt rather than nutty, pull the pan off the heat and keep spooning.

instructions.title: Check the temperature
instructions.text: Slide an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part from the side. For medium, with a rosy, silky center, pull at 125-130°F (52-54°C); the FDA guideline for fully cooked fish is 145°F (63°C), which gives a firmer, flakier fillet. Salmon carries over about 5°F (3°C) off the heat, so take it out a few degrees early.

instructions.title: Rest and serve skin side up
instructions.text: Rest the fillets on a warm plate skin side up for 2 to 3 minutes so the juices redistribute — never on a paper towel or under foil, both of which will steam the crust soft. Squeeze the lemon half over the flesh, finish with the 1/2 tsp flaky salt, and serve with the wedges. Spoon the thyme butter from the pan over the flesh, not the skin.

tips: Farmed Atlantic salmon is fattier and more forgiving; wild sockeye and coho are leaner and go from perfect to dry in a minute, so pull them 5°F (3°C) earlier.
If the skin sticks when you try to flip, it is not ready. Give it another 30-45 seconds and it will release on its own.
Leftover salmon is excellent cold. Flake it into a salad or mash it with mayo, lemon, and dill for a sandwich rather than reheating it, which dries it out.
A splatter screen keeps this from becoming a cleanup project. Skip the lid, though, which traps steam and ruins the skin in seconds.
The same method works for arctic char, steelhead trout, and branzino fillets, all of which cook slightly faster.
recipes.keyTemp: Pull at 125-130°F (52-54°C) for a rosy medium center; the FDA fully-cooked guideline for fish is 145°F (63°C).
recipes.pairing: Pinot Noir or a dry rosé, with roasted potatoes and a lemony green salad.

recipes.title: Blackened Mahi Mahi
recipes.blurb: A dark, spicy crust from a screaming cast iron pan and a fillet that stays sweet and juicy underneath. Open a window, and make the Gulf Coast classic properly.

items: 4 skinless mahi mahi fillets, 6 oz (170 g) each, about 3/4 in (2 cm) thick
6 tbsp (85 g) unsalted butter, melted, plus 2 tbsp (30 g) for finishing
1 lemon (about 4 oz / 115 g), cut into wedges
2 tbsp (8 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley

instructions.title: Mix the spice blend
instructions.text: Whisk the paprika, 1 1/2 tsp salt, garlic powder, onion powder, thyme, oregano, cayenne, black pepper, and white pepper together in a shallow bowl. Crush the dried thyme and oregano between your palms as you add them to release their oils. Blackening is not about burning the fish — it is about toasting these spices in butter until they turn dark and smell like the inside of a good seafood shack.

instructions.title: Prep the fish
instructions.text: Pat the mahi fillets completely dry with paper towels on all sides. If any fillet is much thicker than 1 in (2.5 cm) at one end, slice it horizontally or fold the thin tail under so everything is roughly even. Uneven fillets are the reason one piece comes out perfect and the next comes out dry.

instructions.title: Open a window first
instructions.text: Turn your exhaust fan to high, open a window, and if you have a smoke detector directly above the stove, be ready for it. This technique genuinely smokes — that is where the flavor comes from. If your kitchen has no ventilation at all, do this on a grill side burner or outdoors on a camp stove instead.

instructions.title: Preheat the cast iron
instructions.text: Set a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron skillet over high heat and leave it there for 6 to 8 full minutes with nothing in it. The pan is ready when a drop of water flicked onto the surface skitters and vanishes instantly rather than sitting and boiling. A thin or lightweight pan will not hold enough heat and the fish will steam instead of blacken.

instructions.title: Butter the fish, not the pan
instructions.text: Dip each fillet in the 6 tbsp melted butter, coating both sides completely and letting the excess drip back into the bowl. The butter carries the spices onto the fish and its milk solids are what blacken in the pan. Do not add oil or butter directly to the skillet — it will scorch and smoke before the fish goes in.

instructions.title: Coat heavily with the spices
instructions.text: Press each buttered fillet into the spice mixture on both sides, pressing firmly so a thick, even coat sticks — you want the fish fully covered, not dusted. Use all the seasoning across the four fillets; a thin coat gives you a spicy fish instead of a proper crust. Set them on a plate ready to go, because from here it moves quickly.

instructions.title: Lay the fillets down
instructions.text: Set the fillets in the dry hot skillet away from you, leaving 1 in (2.5 cm) between them, and do not touch them for 2 to 3 minutes. The pan will smoke heavily and the sound should be a loud, constant sizzle. Cook in two batches if all four will not fit with space — crowding drops the heat and you lose the crust.

instructions.title: Flip once
instructions.text: Slide a thin metal spatula under a fillet and lift a corner to look: the crust should be deep mahogany brown with black flecks, not gray and not uniformly charcoal. Flip and cook the second side 2 to 3 minutes more. Mahi at 3/4 in (2 cm) thick needs about 5 minutes total, so resist the urge to keep flipping and checking.

instructions.title: Check doneness
instructions.text: The fish is done at 145°F (63°C) at the thickest point, or when a fork twisted into the center flakes the meat cleanly and it is opaque throughout. Mahi is lean and firm and turns dry and cottony if you push much past that. If a fillet is thicker than the rest, move it to a 400°F (205°C) oven for 2 to 3 minutes rather than leaving it in the pan.

instructions.title: Finish with butter and lemon
instructions.text: Move the fillets to warm plates and top each with a small knob of the remaining 2 tbsp butter so it melts into the crust. Scatter the parsley over the top and serve with lemon wedges. The cold butter and the squeeze of lemon tame the cayenne and turn the spice crust into a sauce.

instructions.title: Clean the pan while it is hot
instructions.text: Carefully pour off any burnt spice, run the still-warm skillet under hot water, and scrub with a stiff brush or chain mail — no soap needed on well-seasoned cast iron. Dry it on the burner over low heat for 2 minutes and wipe with a teaspoon of oil. Blackening leaves behind carbon that is far harder to remove once it cools and sets.

tips: Redfish is the original for this dish and works exactly the same way. Snapper, grouper, catfish, and even chicken breast pounded thin all take the same seasoning and timing.
Cut the cayenne to 1/4 tsp for a milder crust — you will still get all the color and the toasted-spice flavor, just less heat.
The spice blend keeps for 6 months in a sealed jar. Make a triple batch now and you are ten minutes from dinner any night.
Do not use a nonstick pan for this. The temperatures involved are above what nonstick coatings are rated for and they break down.
Serve with something cool and creamy — a slaw, a rice pilaf, or a spoonful of sour cream — to balance the heat.
recipes.keyTemp: Cook to 145°F (63°C) at the thickest point; the fish should flake with a fork and be opaque all the way through.
recipes.pairing: An ice-cold light beer or a citrusy Sauvignon Blanc, with dirty rice and a crunchy slaw.

recipes.title: Low Country Shrimp Boil
recipes.blurb: Shrimp, sausage, corn, and potatoes cooked in one seasoned pot and dumped straight onto a newspaper-covered table. It is less a recipe than a way to feed people you like.

items: 1 bottle (12 oz / 355 ml) light lager beer, optional
1/2 cup (60 g) Old Bay seasoning, plus 2 tbsp for finishing
1 large yellow onion (about 10 oz / 280 g), quartered
1 1/2 lb (680 g) small red potatoes, about 1 1/2 in (4 cm) across
1 lb (450 g) smoked andouille or kielbasa, cut into 2 in (5 cm) lengths
4 ears fresh corn, husked and halved
2 lb (900 g) large shell-on shrimp (16-20 count), deveined if you like
1 lemon (about 4 oz / 115 g), cut into wedges

instructions.title: Build the seasoned broth
instructions.text: Combine the 4 qt water, the beer if using, 1/2 cup Old Bay, 1/4 cup kosher salt, the halved lemons squeezed in and dropped in, the garlic head, quartered onion, and bay leaves in a 12 qt (11 L) stockpot. Bring it to a rolling boil over high heat, which takes about 15 minutes. The water should taste aggressively seasoned, almost too salty to drink — this is the only chance you have to season the food from the inside.

instructions.title: Let it steep
instructions.text: Once it hits a boil, drop to a strong simmer and let the aromatics steep for 10 minutes before any food goes in. Old Bay dumped in at the last minute sits on the surface instead of flavoring anything. You will smell it fill the kitchen when it is ready.

instructions.title: Start the potatoes
instructions.text: Add the 1 1/2 lb red potatoes and return to a boil, then cook 12 to 15 minutes. They are the longest cooking item, so they go first and everything else is timed off them. Test with a paring knife — it should slide into the center with only slight resistance, since they will keep cooking in the residual heat.

instructions.title: Add the sausage
instructions.text: Add the 1 lb of andouille and cook 5 minutes. The sausage is already cooked, so this is about warming it through and letting its smoky paprika-heavy fat bleed into the broth, which seasons everything that follows. Keep the pot at a steady boil the whole time.

instructions.title: Add the corn
instructions.text: Add the 8 half-ears of corn and cook 5 minutes more. Fresh summer corn is sweet enough to eat raw and only needs to be heated through. If you press a kernel with your thumbnail it should burst with milky juice rather than feeling starchy.

instructions.title: Kill the heat before the shrimp
instructions.text: Turn the burner completely off, then add the 2 lb of shrimp and stir once to submerge them. This is the most important step in the recipe. Shrimp cook in 2 to 3 minutes in water that is off the boil, and if you leave the flame on you will have rubber before you can drain the pot.

instructions.title: Watch the shrimp closely
instructions.text: Cover the pot and let the shrimp sit for 2 to 3 minutes, checking at 2. They are done when the shells have turned coral pink, the flesh at the thick end is opaque, and they have curled into a loose C. Pull one out and cut into it if you are unsure — an extra 30 seconds of watching beats two pounds of overcooked shrimp.

instructions.title: Drain immediately
instructions.text: Set a large colander in the sink or use a spider strainer and get everything out of the water the second the shrimp are done. Residual heat in 4 quarts of hot broth will keep cooking the shrimp for several minutes. Discard the lemon halves, onion, garlic, and bay leaves as you go.

instructions.title: Season and toss
instructions.text: Dump everything into a very large bowl or straight onto a table lined with newspaper or parchment. Drizzle with the 8 tbsp melted butter, sprinkle the remaining 2 tbsp Old Bay over the top, and scatter the parsley. Toss gently with your hands or two spoons so the butter and seasoning coat everything.

instructions.title: Serve family style
instructions.text: Put out lemon wedges, cocktail sauce, extra melted butter for dipping, plenty of paper towels, and a bowl for the shells. Serve while everything is still hot, with cold beer and no plates if you are doing it right. Eating with your hands over a covered table is the entire tradition here.

instructions.title: Save the broth
instructions.text: Strain and cool the leftover cooking liquid, then freeze it in quart containers for up to 3 months. It makes a superb base for gumbo, shrimp and grits, or the cioppino in this chapter. Cool it in a shallow pan first so it drops below 40°F (4°C) within two hours.

tips: Shell-on shrimp are worth the mess. The shells protect the meat from the hot water and add real flavor to the broth as everything cooks.
Scale by the pot: figure roughly 1/3 lb (150 g) shrimp, 1/4 lb (115 g) sausage, 1 half-ear of corn, and 4 oz (115 g) potatoes per person.
If your potatoes are bigger than 2 in (5 cm), halve them so they cook in the same 15 minutes. Mismatched sizes are the usual reason something comes out raw in the middle.
Add 2 lb (900 g) of live crawfish or snow crab clusters with the corn for a bigger spread — they need about 5 minutes.
Everything can be prepped hours ahead. Potatoes scrubbed, sausage cut, corn husked, shrimp in a bowl on ice, and the pot goes from cold to table in 45 minutes.
recipes.keyTemp: Shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C) — pink shells, opaque flesh, loose C shape. Potatoes should offer no resistance to a paring knife.
recipes.pairing: Cold light beer or sweet tea, with plenty of paper towels and nothing else on the table.

recipes.title: Mussels in White Wine and Garlic
recipes.blurb: Moules mariniere the way a bistro does it — shallots, wine, butter, and a pile of shells over a broth you will fight over. Twenty minutes, and cheaper than almost anything else in this chapter.
recipes.servings: 2 servings as a main, 4 as a starter

items: 4 lb (1.8 kg) live mussels, preferably farmed rope-grown
2 large shallots (about 4 oz / 115 g), finely diced
1 1/2 cups (360 ml) dry white wine such as Muscadet or Sauvignon Blanc
1/2 cup (20 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 lemon (about 4 oz / 115 g), cut into wedges
1 baguette (about 12 oz / 340 g), sliced thick and toasted

instructions.title: Keep them alive until you cook
instructions.text: Mussels are sold alive and must stay that way until they hit the pot. Store them in the fridge in a bowl covered with a damp towel, never sealed in a plastic bag or sitting in fresh water, both of which suffocate them. Cook them the day you buy them, or the next day at the latest.

instructions.title: Sort and tap test
instructions.text: Tip the mussels into a colander and look them over. Any shell that is cracked or crushed goes in the trash. Any that is gaping open, tap firmly on the counter — a live mussel will slowly draw its shell closed within 30 seconds, and one that stays open is dead and gets thrown out. This takes five minutes and it is the whole safety step for this dish.

instructions.title: Scrub and debeard
instructions.text: Rinse the mussels under cold running water, scrubbing away any grit or barnacles with a stiff brush. If you see a fibrous tuft poking out of the shell, grip it and pull firmly toward the hinge end of the shell to tear it free. Farmed mussels usually need very little of this, but wild ones can be beardy — and debearding kills the mussel, so do it right before cooking.

instructions.title: Get everything ready
instructions.text: Dice the shallots, slice the garlic, chop the parsley, and pour the wine before you turn on a burner. This recipe cooks in under ten minutes with no downtime once it starts. Toast the baguette slices now too, under the broiler for 2 minutes a side.

instructions.title: Sweat the shallots
instructions.text: Melt the 3 tbsp butter in a wide 6 qt (5.7 L) Dutch oven or pot with a tight lid over medium heat. Add the shallots and the 1/2 tsp salt and cook 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent but with no color. You want them sweet and melting, not browned — browned shallots make the broth taste heavy.

instructions.title: Add garlic and chile
instructions.text: Add the sliced garlic and 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes and cook just 60 seconds more, stirring constantly, until the garlic smells sweet and is barely blonde. Garlic burns in seconds at this heat and bitter garlic will ruin an entire pot of broth. Have the wine in your other hand.

instructions.title: Reduce the wine
instructions.text: Pour in the 1 1/2 cups white wine, add the thyme sprigs, raise the heat to high, and boil hard for 2 minutes. This burns off the raw alcohol bite and concentrates the wine so the finished broth tastes round rather than sharp. Scrape the bottom of the pot as it bubbles.

instructions.title: Steam the mussels
instructions.text: Add all the mussels at once, clamp the lid on tight, and cook over high heat for 5 to 7 minutes, shaking the pot firmly by the handles once or twice to redistribute them. The mussels on the bottom cook first, so this shake matters. Do not lift the lid before 4 minutes — you need the trapped steam.

instructions.title: Check that they have opened
instructions.text: Lift the lid: nearly all the shells should be wide open with plump orange or cream-colored meat inside. If a third of them are still shut, cover and cook 2 minutes more. Throw away any mussel that is still tightly closed after the rest have opened — it was almost certainly dead before it went in.

instructions.title: Finish the broth
instructions.text: Use a slotted spoon or tongs to pile the mussels into warm serving bowls. If you want a richer broth, stir the 1/2 cup cream into the liquid left in the pot and simmer 1 minute. Taste it — if it is gritty, pour it through a fine strainer, leaving the last tablespoon of sand behind in the pot.

instructions.title: Pour and serve
instructions.text: Stir the 1/2 cup parsley into the broth and ladle it generously over the mussels, then serve immediately with lemon wedges, toasted baguette, and an empty bowl for shells. Eat them the traditional way: use the first empty shell as a pincer to pull the rest of the meat out. Dunk the bread until the broth is gone.

tips: Buy about 1 lb (450 g) of mussels per person for a starter and 2 lb (900 g) for a main. They are mostly shell, and they are usually the cheapest shellfish at the counter.
The old rule about discarding unopened mussels is worth following. A stubborn one can occasionally just be a strong hinge, but it is not worth the gamble.
Swap the wine for 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of light beer for a Belgian version, or use dry hard cider with the cream for a Normandy spin.
Add 1/2 lb (225 g) of littleneck clams with the mussels if you like, but give them a 3 minute head start since they take longer to open.
Leftover broth freezes well and is a beautiful base for a seafood pasta sauce or a quick chowder.
recipes.keyTemp: No thermometer here — mussels are done when the shells open wide, in 5 to 7 minutes. Discard any that stay tightly shut.
recipes.pairing: The same crisp dry white you cooked with, and hot salted fries if you want the full bistro treatment.

recipes.title: Sesame-Crusted Seared Ahi Tuna
recipes.blurb: Ninety seconds a side, a toasted sesame shell, and a cool ruby center. The cooking is the easy part — buying the right piece of tuna is what makes it.

items: 2 sashimi-grade ahi tuna steaks, 6-8 oz (170-225 g) each, 1 1/4 in (3 cm) thick
1 tbsp (15 ml) grapeseed or avocado oil
3 tbsp (45 ml) soy sauce or tamari
1 tsp (3 g) finely grated fresh ginger

instructions.title: Buy tuna you would eat raw
instructions.text: Ask specifically for sashimi-grade or sushi-grade ahi, which means it was handled and frozen to a standard that makes it safe to eat rare. It should be deep ruby to rose, translucent and glossy, with no brown edges, rainbow sheen, or sour smell. If the fishmonger hesitates when you ask whether it can be eaten rare, cook the steaks all the way to 145°F (63°C) instead.

instructions.title: Make the dipping sauce
instructions.text: Whisk the 3 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp rice vinegar, 2 tsp sesame oil, honey, and grated ginger together in a small bowl until the honey dissolves. Stir in the sliced scallion and the wasabi if you are using it. Make this first and let it sit for at least 10 minutes so the ginger has time to bloom into the soy.

instructions.title: Bring the tuna to temperature
instructions.text: Take the steaks out of the fridge 15 minutes before cooking and blot them completely dry on all sides with paper towels. A fridge-cold steak will still be icy in the center after 90 seconds a side, and surface moisture will steam the sesame seeds instead of toasting them. They should feel dry and tacky.

instructions.title: Season the fish
instructions.text: Season the steaks all over with the 1 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper, including the sides. Season a little more generously than feels natural — only a thin outer layer gets cooked and seasoned, and the raw interior stays bare. The salt also helps the sesame seeds stick.

instructions.title: Coat in sesame seeds
instructions.text: Mix the white and black sesame seeds on a plate and press each steak firmly into them, rolling to cover all four faces and both flat sides. Press hard enough that the seeds embed rather than just resting on the surface. A complete, even coat is what gives you that clean striped crust when you slice it.

instructions.title: Heat the pan hard
instructions.text: Set a heavy 10 in (25 cm) skillet over high heat for 2 to 3 minutes, then add the 1 tbsp grapeseed oil and swirl. You want the oil shimmering with the first thread of smoke — this is one of the few times you genuinely want the pan that hot. A cool pan means the heat creeps deep into the steak before the crust forms and you lose the rare center.

instructions.title: Sear the first side
instructions.text: Lay the steaks in the pan away from you and do not move them for 60 to 90 seconds. Listen for a sharp, loud sizzle from the moment they touch down. Watch the side of the steak: you want the pale cooked band to come no more than 1/4 in (6 mm) up from the bottom.

instructions.title: Sear the second side and edges
instructions.text: Flip and sear the second side another 60 to 90 seconds. Then use tongs to stand each steak on its edges, rolling it for about 15 seconds per edge to toast the sesame all the way around. The whole steak should be in the pan for no more than 3 to 3 1/2 minutes.

instructions.title: Rest very briefly
instructions.text: Move the steaks to a cutting board and let them sit for exactly 2 minutes, no longer and no foil. This lets the seared exterior stop cooking inward. Rest it too long and the residual heat will creep further into the center, turning your rare tuna gray and chalky.

instructions.title: Slice against the grain
instructions.text: Look for the faint lines running through the steak and slice across them with a very sharp knife, cutting pieces about 1/4 in (6 mm) thick in single confident strokes. A sawing motion tears the delicate flesh and drags sesame seeds through the ruby center. Wipe the blade between cuts for clean slices.

instructions.title: Plate and serve cold-center
instructions.text: Fan the slices on chilled plates so the outer 1/4 in ring of pale cooked fish frames the deep red center, and pour the dipping sauce into small bowls alongside. Serve right away while the crust is warm and the middle is still cool. Sliced tuna dries out fast, so slice at the table if you can.

tips: Rare tuna is raw in the center. Anyone pregnant, very young, elderly, or immunocompromised should have the steaks cooked through to 145°F (63°C), which takes about 4 minutes per side.
Frozen-at-sea tuna is often a safer and better buy than fresh at the counter. Thaw it overnight in the fridge, still sealed, then dry it very well.
Serve with a cucumber salad, sushi rice, or a pile of dressed greens. Avocado and pickled ginger both belong on the plate.
If your steaks are only 3/4 in (2 cm) thick, cut the sear to 45 seconds a side or you will cook right through the middle.
Leftovers do not reheat. Slice them cold into a salad or a rice bowl the next day instead.
recipes.keyTemp: Rare center reads about 110°F (43°C) with a 1/4 in cooked band; the FDA fully-cooked guideline for fish is 145°F (63°C). Use sashimi-grade tuna if serving rare.
recipes.pairing: Chilled sake, a dry Riesling, or a cold lager, with steamed rice and cucumber salad.

recipes.title: Beer-Battered Fish and Chips
recipes.blurb: Shatteringly crisp battered cod and proper double-fried chips, the way a good chippy in England does it. It is a project, but the payoff is fish you cannot get from a restaurant near you.

items: 2 1/2 lb (1.1 kg) russet potatoes, peeled and cut into 1/2 in (1.3 cm) batons
2 qt (2 L) peanut, canola, or vegetable oil, for frying
1 tbsp (18 g) kosher salt, for finishing
1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt, for the soaking water
2 lb (900 g) skinless cod or haddock loin, cut into 6 oz (170 g) pieces
1 1/2 cups (190 g) all-purpose flour, plus 1/2 cup (65 g) for dredging
12 oz (355 ml) very cold lager or pale ale
3 tbsp (30 g) minced dill pickle or cornichons
1 lemon (about 4 oz / 115 g), cut into wedges
2 tbsp (30 ml) malt vinegar, for sprinkling

instructions.title: Soak the potatoes
instructions.text: Cut the potatoes into even 1/2 in (1.3 cm) batons and drop them straight into a bowl of cold water with the 1 tbsp fine sea salt as you go. Soak at least 30 minutes, or up to overnight in the fridge, then change the water once if it looks cloudy. This rinses off surface starch that would otherwise make the chips gummy and cause them to stick together in the fryer.

instructions.title: Make the tartar sauce
instructions.text: Stir the 1 cup mayonnaise, pickles, shallot, 1 tbsp lemon juice, dill, and capers together and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes. Made ahead, the pickle and shallot flavors spread through the mayonnaise instead of sitting in it as separate bites. It keeps a week in the fridge.

instructions.title: Dry the fish and the potatoes
instructions.text: Drain the potatoes and dry them thoroughly in a clean towel — genuinely dry, because water and 350°F (175°C) oil react violently. Blot the cod pieces on all sides with paper towels and check for stray bones. Any moisture on the fish will make the batter slide off in the fryer.

instructions.title: Set up the fry station
instructions.text: Pour the 2 qt oil into a heavy 6 qt (5.7 L) Dutch oven — it should come no more than a third of the way up the sides, leaving room for the bubbling. Clip on a deep-fry thermometer and set two wire racks over sheet pans nearby, plus a spider strainer and tongs. Never fill a pot more than a third full with oil, and never leave hot oil unattended.

instructions.title: Blanch the chips at low heat
instructions.text: Heat the oil to 325°F (163°C) and fry the potatoes in two batches for 5 to 6 minutes each, until they are soft and floppy but still pale blond with no browning. This first fry cooks the interior through and drives out water. Lift them onto a rack and let them cool for at least 20 minutes — they can sit for up to 2 hours.

instructions.title: Mix the batter cold and late
instructions.text: Whisk the 1 1/2 cups flour, cornstarch, baking powder, 1 1/2 tsp salt, and 1/2 tsp pepper in a bowl, then pour in the very cold beer and stir with chopsticks or a fork just until it comes together with a few small lumps. It should be the consistency of thin pancake batter and coat a spoon in a thin veil. Do not whisk it smooth — overmixing builds gluten and gives you a tough, bready crust instead of a shattering one.

instructions.title: Dredge the fish
instructions.text: Put the extra 1/2 cup flour in a shallow dish and toss each piece of cod in it, patting off all the excess so only a fine haze remains. The dry flour gives the wet batter something to grip. Skipping this is the number one reason batter slides off in the oil.

instructions.title: Bring the oil to frying temperature
instructions.text: Raise the oil to 375°F (190°C) for the fish. Too cool and the batter absorbs oil and goes greasy; too hot and the crust darkens before the fish is cooked through. Keep the thermometer in and adjust the burner between batches, since dropping cold food in will pull the temperature down 25 to 50 degrees.

instructions.title: Fry the fish two pieces at a time
instructions.text: Dip a floured piece of cod into the batter, let the excess run off for 3 seconds, then lower it into the oil, holding the end for a couple of seconds before releasing so it sets and does not sink and stick. Fry 2 pieces at a time for 5 to 7 minutes, turning once halfway, until deep golden and crisp. Drain on a wire rack, never on paper towels, which steam the bottom soft.

instructions.title: Check the fish temperature
instructions.text: Slide a thermometer into the thickest part of a fried piece; it should read 145°F (63°C) and the fish should flake into big white curds when you nudge it with a fork. Keep finished pieces warm on a rack in a 200°F (95°C) oven while you fry the rest, up to 20 minutes. Between batches, skim out any loose bits of batter, which burn and taste bitter.

instructions.title: Fry the chips again
instructions.text: Bring the oil back to 375°F (190°C) and fry the blanched potatoes in two batches for 3 to 4 minutes each, until deep golden and audibly crisp when you shake the strainer. The second fry sets a hard, glassy shell around the fluffy interior. Salt them with the 1 tbsp kosher salt the second they come out, while the surface oil can still hold it.

instructions.title: Serve immediately
instructions.text: Pile the fish and chips on a paper-lined tray or plates, sprinkle the malt vinegar over the chips, and serve with the tartar sauce and lemon wedges. This is food with a ten-minute window before the crust starts to soften. Have everyone at the table before the last batch comes out.

tips: Cod and haddock are the classics. Pollock and hake are cheaper and work well; avoid thin, delicate fish like sole, which falls apart in the batter.
Keep the beer in the fridge until the second you pour it. Cold batter hitting hot oil creates a bigger steam burst, which is what makes the crust light and full of bubbles.
Substitute cold club soda or sparkling water for the beer if you want it alcohol free — you lose a little flavor but the texture is nearly identical.
The blanched chips can be fried, cooled, and refrigerated a day ahead, or frozen on a sheet pan and fried straight from frozen. This turns a project into a weeknight.
Let the oil cool completely, strain it through a coffee filter into a jar, and it is good for two or three more fries.
recipes.keyTemp: Fry oil at 325°F (163°C) for the first chip fry and 375°F (190°C) for the fish and the second chip fry. Fish is done at 145°F (63°C) and flakes cleanly.
recipes.pairing: A pint of the same lager you used in the batter, with mushy peas and a lot of malt vinegar.

recipes.title: Baked Cod with Lemon Butter
recipes.blurb: Thick cod loin baked in a lemon-garlic butter that turns into its own sauce in the pan. This is the quiet Tuesday dinner that tastes like you tried much harder than you did.

items: 4 skinless cod loin fillets, 6 oz (170 g) each, about 1 1/4 in (3 cm) thick
3 tbsp (45 ml) fresh lemon juice, plus 1 tsp finely grated zest
3 tbsp (12 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley

instructions.title: Heat the oven and the dish
instructions.text: Position a rack in the upper third of the oven and preheat to 400°F (205°C), giving it a full 15 minutes to come up to temperature. Ovens routinely read hot or cold by 25 degrees, so an oven thermometer is worth the six dollars. A hot oven cooks cod fast enough that it stays juicy rather than slowly weeping liquid into the dish.

instructions.title: Dry and inspect the cod
instructions.text: Pat the fillets completely dry on both sides with paper towels and run a finger over each one, feeling for pin bones or bits of skin. Look for loin cuts — the thick, even front section — rather than the thin tail end, which overcooks in half the time. Frozen-at-sea cod is often the best quality available and should be thawed overnight in the fridge, then dried very well.

instructions.title: Season the fish
instructions.text: Season both sides with the 1 tsp kosher salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, and 1/4 tsp paprika. Let the fillets sit for 10 minutes at room temperature while you make the butter. The paprika is mostly for color, since a baked white fish comes out pale without a little help.

instructions.title: Mix the lemon butter
instructions.text: Stir the 5 tbsp melted butter with the minced garlic, 3 tbsp lemon juice, the zest, capers if using, and 2 tbsp of the parsley. It will look broken and separated, which is fine — it comes together in the pan as the fish releases its juices. Taste it and add a pinch of salt if the lemon feels sharp.

instructions.title: Assemble the baking dish
instructions.text: Choose a baking dish that holds the fillets with about 1 in (2.5 cm) between them, roughly a 9 by 13 in (23 by 33 cm) pan for four pieces. Too large a dish lets the butter spread thin and burn; too small and the fish steams. Lay the lemon slices down first and set the fillets on top so they do not stick.

instructions.title: Pour and top
instructions.text: Spoon the lemon butter evenly over and around the fillets, making sure the tops are well coated. If you want a crisp top, toss the 1/2 cup panko with 1 tbsp of the butter from the dish and press it onto the fillets. The crumb layer is optional but adds a nice contrast against the soft flakes.

instructions.title: Bake without covering
instructions.text: Slide the dish into the upper third of the oven and bake, uncovered, for 12 to 15 minutes for 1 1/4 in (3 cm) fillets. The general rule is about 10 minutes per inch of thickness at this temperature. Covering the dish traps steam and gives you a soggy, poached texture instead of a lightly roasted one.

instructions.title: Baste once at the halfway point
instructions.text: At the 7 minute mark, pull the dish out and spoon the butter from the corners back over the fish, then return it to the oven. This keeps the top from drying and redistributes the garlic, which likes to settle. It takes ten seconds and it is the difference between good and very good.

instructions.title: Test for doneness
instructions.text: The cod is done at 145°F (63°C) at the thickest point, or when the tip of a knife slid into the center meets no resistance and the flakes separate in large opaque curds. Slightly translucent in the very center is fine — it finishes on the plate. Cod goes from silky to dry and chalky in about 90 seconds, so check early.

instructions.title: Rest and sauce
instructions.text: Let the fish sit in the dish for 2 to 3 minutes while the butter, lemon juice, and fish juices pool together into a light pan sauce. Tilt the dish and spoon that sauce over each fillet as you serve. Scatter the remaining 1 tbsp parsley over the top.

instructions.title: Plate with something to soak it up
instructions.text: Move the fillets carefully with a wide spatula — cod is fragile once cooked and will break if you use tongs. Serve over rice, orzo, or crushed potatoes so nothing of that lemon butter is wasted. A roasted green vegetable on the side finishes the plate.

tips: Halibut, haddock, pollock, and striped bass all work in this recipe. Halibut over 1 in (2.5 cm) thick needs 2-3 extra minutes since it is denser than cod.
If your fillets are thin tail pieces under 1 in (2.5 cm), start checking at 8 minutes. Thickness, not weight, determines the time.
Cod releases water as it bakes. If yours looks like it is swimming, the fish was previously frozen and not dried enough — drain the excess before saucing.
The lemon butter can be mixed up to 3 days ahead and refrigerated; melt it gently before using or it will not spread evenly.
Add 1 pint (about 300 g) of cherry tomatoes and 1 bunch of trimmed asparagus to the dish around the fish to make it a sheet pan dinner. Give the vegetables a 6 minute head start.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at 400°F (205°C) until the fish reaches 145°F (63°C) and flakes cleanly with a fork, about 12-15 minutes for 1 1/4 in fillets.
recipes.pairing: A crisp Pinot Grigio or Vinho Verde, with rice pilaf and roasted asparagus.

recipes.title: Coconut Shrimp with Sweet Chili Sauce
recipes.blurb: Big shrimp in a crunchy coconut and panko jacket, fried golden and dunked in sweet chili sauce. They taste like a vacation and disappear faster than you can fry them.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) large shrimp (16-20 count), peeled and deveined, tails on
2 tbsp (30 ml) canned coconut milk or whole milk
6 cups (1.4 L) canola, peanut, or vegetable oil, for frying
1/2 cup (120 ml) Thai sweet chili sauce
1 tbsp (4 g) chopped fresh cilantro, optional

instructions.title: Stir together the sauce
instructions.text: Whisk the 1/2 cup sweet chili sauce, apricot preserves, 1 tbsp lime juice, and 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes in a small bowl until smooth, then stir in the cilantro. The preserves add body so the sauce clings to the shrimp instead of running off, and the lime keeps it from being cloying. Set it aside at room temperature — cold sauce dulls the flavor.

instructions.title: Prep and dry the shrimp
instructions.text: Peel the shrimp but leave the tail segment on, which gives you a handle for dipping and eating. Butterfly each one by cutting about halfway through along the back curve and pressing it open, which makes them lie flat and look twice as big. Blot them completely dry on paper towels — wet shrimp will not hold a breading.

instructions.title: Set up three stations
instructions.text: In the first shallow dish, whisk the 1/2 cup flour with the 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp black pepper, and cayenne. In the second, beat the 2 eggs with the 2 tbsp coconut milk until completely uniform. In the third, toss the 1 1/2 cups shredded coconut with the 1 cup panko — the panko is not traditional but it keeps the coconut from burning and adds real crunch.

instructions.title: Bread with one wet hand
instructions.text: Hold each shrimp by the tail, dredge in flour and shake off every bit of excess, dip in the egg and let it drip for 3 seconds, then press firmly into the coconut mixture on both sides. Use one hand for the dry dishes and one for the egg or you will end up with clubs of batter on your fingers. Set the breaded shrimp on a parchment-lined sheet pan without touching.

instructions.title: Chill the breading
instructions.text: Refrigerate the breaded shrimp uncovered for 15 minutes before frying, or up to 4 hours. This lets the flour hydrate and the coating set so it does not slide off in the oil. It is the same reason breaded cutlets rest before they cook.

instructions.title: Heat the oil to temperature
instructions.text: Pour the 6 cups oil into a heavy 4 qt (3.8 L) pot so it is about 2 in (5 cm) deep and no more than a third of the way up the sides. Clip on a thermometer and heat to 350°F (175°C) over medium-high, which takes about 10 minutes. This is a lower temperature than most frying because sweetened coconut contains sugar and will darken fast.

instructions.title: Test with one shrimp
instructions.text: Fry a single shrimp first and watch it: it should bubble vigorously the second it hits the oil and turn light gold in about 60 seconds. If it browns instantly, drop the heat; if it sits quietly and soaks, raise it. That one test shrimp saves the whole batch.

instructions.title: Fry in small batches
instructions.text: Lower 5 or 6 shrimp into the oil at a time, never crowding, and fry 2 to 3 minutes total, turning once with a spider strainer after about 90 seconds. They are done when the coconut is a warm golden brown and the shrimp have curled into a loose C. Let the oil come back up to 350°F (175°C) between batches, checking the thermometer each time.

instructions.title: Drain on a rack
instructions.text: Lift the shrimp onto a wire rack set over a sheet pan and season with a light pinch of salt right away. Paper towels trap steam under the shrimp and turn the bottom coating soggy within a minute. Keep finished batches warm in a 200°F (95°C) oven for up to 20 minutes.

instructions.title: Check one for doneness
instructions.text: Cut into the thickest shrimp of the first batch — it should be opaque white all the way through with no gray translucent center, which is 145°F (63°C). Large shrimp cook in under 3 minutes, so if the coating is dark before the inside is done, your oil is too hot. Adjust and keep going.

instructions.title: Serve hot with the sauce
instructions.text: Pile the shrimp on a platter with the dipping sauce in the middle and lime wedges around the edge. These are best within ten minutes of leaving the oil, while the coconut still crackles. If they do soften, five minutes on a rack in a 400°F (205°C) oven brings them right back.

tips: Sweetened shredded coconut browns better and tastes more like the restaurant version. Unsweetened works and is less sweet, but watch it closely because it toasts faster.
To bake instead of fry, arrange on a greased rack over a sheet pan, spray generously with oil, and bake at 425°F (220°C) for 12-14 minutes, flipping once. Less crisp but far less work.
An air fryer at 400°F (205°C) for 8-10 minutes works well, but spray the coating with oil or the coconut stays chalky and pale.
Bread the shrimp up to 4 hours ahead and keep them uncovered in the fridge on a sheet pan. Do not stack or cover them or the coating will go soft.
Save 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the frying oil after it cools and strain it — it will taste faintly of coconut and is great for the next batch.
recipes.keyTemp: Fry at 350°F (175°C); shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C) — opaque throughout and curled into a loose C.
recipes.pairing: A cold pilsner or a rum punch, with a crunchy cabbage and lime slaw.

recipes.title: Charleston Shrimp and Grits
recipes.blurb: Slow-cooked cheesy grits under shrimp in a bacon and lemon pan gravy. This is Sunday morning food that is just as good at nine at night.

items: 1 cup (170 g) stone-ground grits, not instant
1 cup (110 g) sharp cheddar, freshly grated
1 1/4 lb (570 g) large shrimp (21-25 count), peeled and deveined
5 slices thick-cut bacon (about 6 oz / 170 g), cut into 1/2 in pieces
3/4 cup (180 ml) chicken or seafood stock
1 tsp (5 ml) hot sauce such as Crystal or Tabasco

instructions.title: Rinse and skim the grits
instructions.text: Put the 1 cup of stone-ground grits in a bowl, cover with cold water, swish, and pour off the chaff and hulls that float to the top. Real stone-ground grits carry bits of the corn hull that can taste bitter and never soften. Drain them well in a fine sieve — this takes two minutes and improves the texture noticeably.

instructions.title: Start the grits low and slow
instructions.text: Bring the 2 cups water, 2 cups milk, and 1 1/2 tsp salt to a bare simmer in a heavy 3 qt (2.8 L) saucepan, then rain the grits in while whisking constantly. Whisking as they go in is what prevents lumps, which you cannot whisk out later. Once they start to thicken, drop the heat to the lowest setting your stove has.

instructions.title: Cook and stir for 35 minutes
instructions.text: Cover and cook the grits 30 to 40 minutes, stirring well with a wooden spoon every 5 minutes and scraping the bottom corners of the pan where they catch and scorch. They are done when each grain is fully tender with no chalky center and the mixture falls slowly from the spoon in a thick ribbon. If they get too thick before they are tender, whisk in hot water 1/4 cup (60 ml) at a time.

instructions.title: Season the shrimp
instructions.text: While the grits cook, pat the shrimp dry and toss with the 1 tsp kosher salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, and 1/2 tsp paprika. Let them sit at room temperature for 15 minutes so they cook evenly. Dry, seasoned shrimp will pick up color in the bacon fat instead of steaming.

instructions.title: Render the bacon
instructions.text: Cook the bacon pieces in a cold 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until crisp and deeply browned. Starting in a cold pan renders the fat slowly instead of seizing the meat, which gives you both crisper bacon and more fat to cook in. Lift the bacon to a paper towel and leave 3 tbsp of the fat in the pan.

instructions.title: Sear the shrimp fast
instructions.text: Raise the heat to medium-high and cook the shrimp in the bacon fat in a single layer for about 60 seconds a side, until pink at the edges but still slightly translucent in the center. Work in two batches if they do not fit with space between them. Move them to a plate immediately — they finish in the gravy and will turn rubbery if you cook them fully now.

instructions.title: Build the gravy
instructions.text: Lower the heat to medium, add the minced garlic to the pan, and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant but not brown. Sprinkle the 1 tbsp flour over the fat and cook, stirring, for 1 minute — you are making a small blond roux that will thicken the gravy and take away the raw flour taste. It should smell faintly like toast.

instructions.title: Deglaze and simmer
instructions.text: Pour in the 3/4 cup stock while whisking, scraping up every browned bit from the bottom of the pan. Simmer 2 to 3 minutes until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon and leaves a clear line when you draw a finger through it. If it gets too thick, loosen it with another splash of stock.

instructions.title: Finish the grits with cheese
instructions.text: Off the heat, beat the 4 tbsp butter into the finished grits until it disappears, then add the 1 cup grated cheddar in two handfuls, stirring until smooth, and season with the 1/4 tsp pepper. Grate the cheese yourself — pre-shredded is coated in starch that makes grits grainy. Taste for salt; grits need more than you expect.

instructions.title: Bring the shrimp back
instructions.text: Add the 2 tbsp lemon juice, the hot sauce, the shrimp with any juices on the plate, and most of the bacon to the gravy. Toss over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes, just until the shrimp are opaque throughout at 145°F (63°C) and curled into a loose C. Taste the gravy and adjust the lemon and hot sauce.

instructions.title: Serve in warm bowls
instructions.text: Spoon a generous ladle of grits into each warm bowl and make a shallow well in the center with the back of the spoon. Pile the shrimp and gravy into the well and scatter the reserved bacon and the sliced scallions over the top. Serve immediately, because grits set up like concrete as they cool.

tips: Instant or quick grits will work in a pinch, following their package timing, but stone-ground grits are the whole point of this dish. Anson Mills and Geechie Boy are worth ordering.
Leftover grits set firm in the fridge. Cut them into squares and pan-fry in butter until crisp for one of the best breakfasts there is.
If your grits go lumpy, an immersion blender for 10 seconds saves them. Do not overdo it or they turn gluey.
Buy shell-on shrimp and simmer the shells in the 3/4 cup stock for 15 minutes, then strain. It costs you nothing and makes the gravy taste like a restaurant made it.
The grits can be made up to 2 days ahead. Reheat over low heat with a splash of milk, whisking until they loosen back up.
recipes.keyTemp: Shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C) — opaque and loosely curled. Grits are ready when each grain is tender with no chalky center, about 35 minutes.
recipes.pairing: A cold beer or a Bloody Mary, with hot sauce on the table and nothing else required.
