recipes.title: San Francisco Cioppino
recipes.blurb: A big red tomato and wine broth loaded with clams, mussels, shrimp, and fish, invented by Italian fishermen in North Beach. Serve it with bread and a stack of napkins.

items: 1 large fennel bulb (about 12 oz / 340 g), cored and thinly sliced
1 large yellow onion (about 10 oz / 280 g), diced
1 1/2 cups (360 ml) dry white wine such as Pinot Grigio
1 can (28 oz / 795 g) crushed San Marzano tomatoes
3 cups (720 ml) fish stock or bottled clam juice
1 lb (450 g) mussels, scrubbed and debearded
1 lb (450 g) large shrimp (16-20 count), peeled and deveined, shells reserved
1 lb (450 g) firm white fish such as halibut, cod, or sea bass, cut into 1 1/2 in (4 cm) chunks
8 oz (225 g) sea scallops, side muscle removed, optional
1 cooked Dungeness crab (about 2 lb / 900 g), cleaned and cracked, optional
1/2 cup (20 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 lemon (about 4 oz / 115 g), cut into wedges
1 loaf (about 1 lb / 450 g) sourdough bread, sliced and grilled

instructions.title: Purge and check the shellfish
instructions.text: Soak the clams in a bowl of cold salted water — 1 tbsp (18 g) salt per quart (950 ml) — for 20 to 30 minutes so they spit out their sand, then lift them out rather than pouring, leaving the grit behind. Scrub and debeard the mussels, and tap any gaping shell on the counter; if it does not slowly close within 30 seconds, throw it away. Discard anything cracked. Sandy cioppino is the classic failure of this dish.

instructions.title: Make a quick shrimp stock
instructions.text: If you bought shell-on shrimp, simmer the shells in the 3 cups of fish stock or clam juice for 15 minutes, then strain and discard the shells. This costs you nothing and adds a sweet shellfish depth that bottled clam juice alone does not have. Keep the stock warm on a back burner.

instructions.title: Sweat the fennel and onion
instructions.text: Heat the 1/4 cup olive oil in a 7 qt (6.6 L) Dutch oven over medium heat and add the sliced fennel, diced onion, and 2 tsp kosher salt. Cook 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often, until everything is completely soft and translucent with just a little golden color at the edges. Do not rush this on high heat — the sweetness that develops here is the backbone of the broth.

instructions.title: Bloom the garlic and chile
instructions.text: Add the minced garlic and 1 tsp red pepper flakes and cook 1 minute more, stirring constantly, until the garlic smells sweet and the chile perfumes the oil. Fat-soluble flavors need hot oil to release, which is why this happens before any liquid goes in. Watch it closely; garlic burns in seconds.

instructions.title: Caramelize the tomato paste
instructions.text: Stir in the 2 tbsp tomato paste and cook it for 2 to 3 minutes, smearing it against the bottom of the pot, until it darkens from bright red to a deep brick color. This step drives off the tinny raw taste and builds a savory backbone. It should smell rich and slightly sweet, not sharp.

instructions.title: Deglaze with wine
instructions.text: Pour in the 1 1/2 cups white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot hard with a wooden spoon to release everything stuck there. Boil for 4 to 5 minutes until reduced by about half and the harsh alcohol smell is gone. If you can still smell raw wine, keep going — this stew has nowhere to hide it.

instructions.title: Simmer the broth
instructions.text: Add the crushed tomatoes, the warm stock, bay leaves, oregano, and the saffron if using. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer with the lid ajar and cook 30 to 40 minutes, stirring occasionally. The broth should reduce slightly and taste round and unified rather than like tomatoes and wine sitting next to each other. Taste and adjust the salt now, because you cannot stir the pot much once the seafood is in.

instructions.title: Get everything ready to go in
instructions.text: Cut the fish into even 1 1/2 in (4 cm) chunks, pat the shrimp and scallops dry, and have all the shellfish within arm's reach of the stove. From this point the whole thing takes about 12 minutes and each item goes in on a timer. Set out warm bowls and grill your bread now.

instructions.title: Clams first
instructions.text: Bring the broth to a strong simmer, add the clams and the crab pieces if using, cover, and cook 5 minutes. Clams have the thickest shells and take the longest to open, which is why they lead. Do not stir the pot from here on — use the lid and the simmer to move the heat around.

instructions.title: Then mussels and fish
instructions.text: Add the mussels and the chunks of white fish, nestling the fish into the broth without stirring, cover, and cook 3 minutes. The fish is fragile and stirring will break it into shreds. You should see most of the mussel shells beginning to gap open.

instructions.title: Shrimp and scallops last
instructions.text: Scatter the shrimp and scallops over the top, cover, and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, until the shrimp are pink and curled and the scallops are just opaque. Everything in the pot should now be done at once. Discard any clams or mussels that are still tightly shut.

instructions.title: Check and finish
instructions.text: The fish should flake at 145°F (63°C) and the shrimp should be opaque at 145°F (63°C). Turn off the heat, stir in the 1/2 cup parsley and the basil as gently as you can, and taste one last time for salt and heat. A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the whole pot.

instructions.title: Serve in wide bowls
instructions.text: Ladle into warm wide bowls, making sure everyone gets some of each kind of seafood and plenty of broth. Serve with grilled sourdough, lemon wedges, an empty bowl for shells, and a bib if you own one. This is a stew you eat with your hands and a spoon at the same time.

tips: The tomato broth is the make-ahead half of this dish. Make it up to 3 days ahead or freeze it for 3 months, then reheat and add seafood the night you serve it.
Use whatever is good and fresh at the counter. Squid, halibut cheeks, king crab legs, and rockfish all belong here; skip delicate flounder, which disintegrates.
The order matters more than the exact species: thickest shells first, then fish, then shrimp and scallops last. That is the whole technique.
If the broth tastes flat, it needs salt or acid before it needs anything else. Try 1/2 tsp of salt or a squeeze of lemon before reaching for more herbs.
Grill the bread with olive oil and a raw garlic clove rubbed over the hot surface. It sounds fussy and takes 90 seconds.
recipes.keyTemp: Fish and shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C); clams and mussels are done when their shells open wide. Discard any shellfish that stays shut.
recipes.pairing: A bold Italian white or a light Sangiovese, with grilled sourdough and a green salad after.

recipes.title: Grilled Swordfish with Salmoriglio
recipes.blurb: Meaty swordfish steaks over a hot grill, finished with the Sicilian lemon, oregano, and olive oil sauce called salmoriglio. It eats like a steak but cooks in ten minutes.

items: 4 swordfish steaks, 6-8 oz (170-225 g) each, 1 in (2.5 cm) thick
2 tsp dried oregano, preferably Sicilian on the branch
2 tbsp (8 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley

instructions.title: Pick good steaks
instructions.text: Look for swordfish that is firm, moist, and pale ivory to pink with a tight, close grain and no gaps between the muscle layers. The dark bloodline running through one edge is normal but strong tasting, so trim it if you are sensitive to it. Steaks under 3/4 in (2 cm) thick dry out on a grill, so ask the counter to cut them a full inch.

instructions.title: Marinate briefly
instructions.text: Rub the steaks with the 3 tbsp olive oil, smashed garlic, 1 tsp dried oregano, the lemon zest, 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, and 3/4 tsp pepper, then let them sit at room temperature for 20 minutes. Do not add lemon juice to the marinade and do not go longer than 30 minutes — acid starts to cure the surface of the fish and turns it opaque and mealy before it ever hits heat.

instructions.title: Whisk the salmoriglio
instructions.text: In a bowl, whisk the 3 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp warm water, grated garlic, 1/2 tsp salt, and 2 tsp oregano, then drizzle in the 1/3 cup olive oil while whisking until it thickens slightly and looks creamy. The warm water is the traditional trick that helps it emulsify. Stir in the parsley and red pepper flakes and let it sit 15 minutes for the oregano to soften.

instructions.title: Get the grill hot and clean
instructions.text: Heat a gas grill on high or build a charcoal fire for direct high heat, aiming for around 500°F (260°C) at the grate, and give it 10 to 15 minutes with the lid closed. Scrape the grates with a wire brush until they are shiny, then oil them by wiping with a tongs-held paper towel dipped in neutral oil. Clean and oiled grates are the only reason fish does not stick.

instructions.title: Blot the fish before it goes on
instructions.text: Wipe the excess marinade off the steaks with a paper towel, leaving them lightly oiled but not dripping. Excess oil causes flare-ups that char the outside and leave the middle raw. Discard the smashed garlic, which would burn on the grate.

instructions.title: Lay the steaks down and leave them
instructions.text: Set the steaks on the hottest part of the grate at a 45 degree angle to the bars and close the lid. Cook 4 to 5 minutes without touching them — you should hear a steady sizzle and see the edges turn opaque and creep upward. Moving the fish before a crust forms is what tears it apart.

instructions.title: Flip once with confidence
instructions.text: Slide a wide metal spatula fully under a steak and lift; if it resists, give it another 30 seconds and it will release. Flip and grill the second side 3 to 4 minutes. Swordfish is dense and forgiving compared to flaky fish, but it still only wants about 8 to 9 minutes total for a 1 in steak.

instructions.title: Check the temperature early
instructions.text: Slide an instant-read thermometer in from the side into the center. The FDA guideline for fully cooked fish is 145°F (63°C); many cooks pull swordfish at 130-135°F (54-57°C) for a moister, faintly pink center and let carryover do the rest. Swordfish is lean and dries out fast, so start checking at the 7 minute mark.

instructions.title: Rest the steaks
instructions.text: Move the steaks to a warm platter and let them rest 3 to 5 minutes, loosely tented if your kitchen is cold. Like beef, swordfish is muscular enough that resting lets the juices settle back through the meat instead of running out onto the plate. They will climb about 5°F (3°C) as they sit.

instructions.title: Sauce at the table
instructions.text: Whisk the salmoriglio once more to bring it back together and spoon it generously over the rested steaks. Do not sauce them before resting or the lemon will make the surface soggy. Any leftover sauce is excellent on grilled vegetables or bread.

instructions.title: Serve with something charred
instructions.text: While the fish rests, throw halved lemons, zucchini planks, or thick tomato slices on the still-hot grate for 2 to 3 minutes. Grilled lemon squeezed over the fish at the table is sweeter and rounder than raw. Serve everything family style on one big platter.

tips: No grill? A cast iron grill pan or a heavy skillet over medium-high heat gives you the same result. Preheat it for 5 minutes and use the same timing.
Mahi mahi, tuna, halibut steaks, and thick salmon fillets all work with this method and this sauce.
Salmoriglio keeps 3 days in the fridge, but the garlic gets sharper each day. Bring it back to room temperature and whisk before serving.
If a steak has a tough band of skin around the outside, cut through it in two or three places so the steak does not curl on the grill.
Swordfish is a high-mercury fish. It is worth knowing if you are pregnant or feeding small children, in which case cod or salmon is the better choice for this dish.
recipes.keyTemp: Grill to 145°F (63°C) for the FDA fully-cooked guideline; pull at 130-135°F (54-57°C) for a moister, faintly pink center.
recipes.pairing: A chilled Sicilian white like Grillo, with grilled vegetables and roasted potatoes.

recipes.title: Seafood Paella with Saffron Rice
recipes.blurb: Saffron rice cooked flat and undisturbed until a crackling golden crust forms on the bottom, crowded with shrimp, mussels, and squid. This is the weekend showpiece of the chapter.

items: 5 cups (1.2 L) fish or shellfish stock
1 large yellow onion (about 10 oz / 280 g), finely diced
1 red bell pepper (about 6 oz / 170 g), cut into strips
1 1/2 cups (270 g) grated fresh tomato, or canned crushed tomatoes
2 cups (400 g) bomba, Calasparra, or other Spanish short-grain rice
1 lb (450 g) large shrimp (16-20 count), shell-on or peeled
1 lb (450 g) mussels or littleneck clams, scrubbed and debearded
8 oz (225 g) cleaned squid, bodies cut into 1/2 in (1.3 cm) rings
1/4 cup (10 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
2 lemons (about 8 oz / 225 g total), cut into wedges

instructions.title: Bloom the saffron
instructions.text: Warm the 5 cups of stock in a saucepan until steaming but not boiling, crumble the 1/2 tsp saffron threads between your fingers, and stir them in. Let it steep at least 10 minutes while you prep everything else, until the liquid glows deep orange-gold. Saffron needs warmth and time to release its color and its honeyed, hay-like aroma, and adding threads directly to the rice wastes most of it.

instructions.title: Prep every ingredient first
instructions.text: Dice the onion, slice the pepper, mince the garlic, grate the tomatoes, scrub the mussels, and cut the squid before you light a burner. Paella has no pauses once it starts, and you cannot stop to chop an onion halfway through. Set everything in bowls around the stove in the order you will use it.

instructions.title: Pick the right pan
instructions.text: Use a 15 in (38 cm) paella pan or the widest, shallowest skillet you own — the goal is rice no more than 1/2 in (1.3 cm) deep, which is what lets it cook without stirring. A deep Dutch oven will give you rice pudding, not paella. If your burner is smaller than the pan, plan to rotate it every few minutes so the whole base heats evenly.

instructions.title: Sear the seafood and pull it out
instructions.text: Heat the 1/4 cup olive oil over medium-high and sear the shrimp for 60 seconds a side and the squid for about 60 seconds total, just until they take on a little color. Move both to a plate — they are only 70 percent cooked and will finish on top of the rice at the end. Cooking them now leaves shellfish flavor in the oil that carries through the whole dish.

instructions.title: Build the sofrito
instructions.text: Lower the heat to medium, add the onion, bell pepper, and 2 tsp salt to the same pan, and cook 8 to 10 minutes until very soft and lightly golden. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more. This slow-cooked vegetable base is called sofrito and it is where most of the flavor in a paella actually lives, so do not shortcut it.

instructions.title: Add paprika and tomato
instructions.text: Stir in the 2 tsp smoked paprika and cook for just 30 seconds — paprika scorches almost instantly and turns acrid. Immediately add the 1 1/2 cups grated tomato and cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the mixture darkens to brick red and the oil separates and pools at the edges. That separation is your signal the sofrito is finished.

instructions.title: Toast the rice
instructions.text: Add the 2 cups of rice and stir for 2 minutes so every grain is coated in the oil and sofrito. Toasting the exterior of the grain helps it stay separate and absorb liquid evenly instead of turning creamy. Spread the rice into a flat, even layer across the whole pan.

instructions.title: Add the stock and stop stirring
instructions.text: Pour in all 5 cups of the saffron stock, shake the pan gently to level the rice, and bring it to a strong boil. From this moment on, do not stir the rice again — stirring releases starch and makes risotto, and it destroys the crust you are building. Taste the broth now and add salt if it needs it; this is your last chance to season.

instructions.title: Boil hard, then simmer
instructions.text: Boil hard for 5 minutes, rotating the pan a quarter turn every minute or two if your burner is smaller than the pan. Then reduce to a steady medium-low simmer and cook 10 minutes more, uncovered. You should see the liquid level dropping to just below the surface of the rice.

instructions.title: Add the shellfish
instructions.text: Nestle the mussels or clams hinge-down into the rice so they will open upward and keep their juices, and scatter the peas over the top. Cook 5 minutes more, until the shells open wide. Any shell still shut at the end gets thrown out.

instructions.title: Return the shrimp and squid
instructions.text: Arrange the seared shrimp and squid over the surface of the rice and cook 3 to 5 minutes more, until the shrimp are opaque at 145°F (63°C) and the rice is tender with no chalky center. Taste a grain from the middle of the pan rather than the edge. If the rice is still hard and the pan is dry, add 1/4 cup (60 ml) of hot stock around the edges.

instructions.title: Make the socarrat
instructions.text: Turn the heat to high for 60 to 90 seconds and listen closely — you want a crackling, popping sound and the smell of toasting rice, but stop the second it smells sharp or burnt. This forms the socarrat, the caramelized crust of rice on the bottom of the pan that is the most prized part of the dish. Scrape gently with a spoon at the edge to check for a golden brown layer.

instructions.title: Rest before serving
instructions.text: Take the pan off the heat, cover it loosely with a clean kitchen towel or foil, and let it rest 10 minutes. The rice finishes absorbing the last of the liquid and firms up so it does not fall apart when you serve it. Skipping this rest is why home paella often tastes wet.

instructions.title: Serve from the pan
instructions.text: Uncover, scatter the 1/4 cup parsley and the 1/2 tsp flaky salt over the top, and tuck the lemon wedges around the edge. Bring the whole pan to the table and let everyone serve themselves straight from it, digging down for a piece of the crust. Traditionally people eat from the wedge of the pan directly in front of them.

tips: Bomba rice absorbs three times its volume in liquid without falling apart, which is why the ratio here is 2 1/2 cups of stock per cup of rice. Arborio works but needs about 1/2 cup less liquid and turns creamier.
Do not use long-grain or basmati rice. It will not absorb the broth the same way and you will never get a socarrat.
Homemade stock from shrimp shells simmered 20 minutes with an onion, a bay leaf, and 6 cups of water is a huge upgrade over bottled clam juice.
If your stovetop cannot heat the whole pan evenly, finish the paella uncovered in a 400°F (205°C) oven for the last 10 minutes, then do the socarrat over a burner for 90 seconds.
Leftovers reheat surprisingly well in a covered skillet with a splash of stock over low heat, or make excellent arancini-style rice cakes the next day.
recipes.keyTemp: Shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C); mussels and clams are done when they open wide. The rice should be tender with no chalky center and a crisp golden socarrat underneath.
recipes.pairing: A cold Spanish rosado or dry cava, with an olive oil and sherry vinegar green salad.
